name: Integrity
label: Victory
lede: Dwid Hellion was printing T-shirts for an invented straight edge band when he decided to make it real. Integrity went on to the darkest corner of Victory Records, and moved to Belgium after its singer met a girl on tour.

eras.title: Merch first, band second
eras.text: Dwid Hellion invented bands as a teenager, and one of them was billed as the most violent straight edge band alive. In 1988 he made it real in Cleveland, and its first album split hardcore down the middle.

years.h: Dwid Hellion grows up on an Indiana farm, listening to Delta blues
years.p: His grandparents raised him near La Fontaine, Indiana. Alan Lomax's chain gang recordings stuck, and then skating and Thrasher's music pages pointed him to punk.

years.h: Dwid Hellion turns a T-shirt band into a real one
years.p: After his youth crew band Die Hard broke up, Hellion recruited guitarist Aaron Melnick, drummer Tony "Chubby Fresh" Pines and bassist Tom Front. They kept the name he'd already put on shirts.
years.xp:
Hellion spent his teens inventing bands, drawing their merch and spreading their backstories. Integrity was billed as a straight edge band so violent it would attack drinkers at shows. The logo came off the cover of a book called Integrity from a secondhand shop.

He told Thrasher the first members came out of a skate crew: "We called ourselves Team Playboy because we found a big pack of Playboy stickers." The name Dwid, he said, came from a drunken slur when he was 13.

years.h: Leon Melnick, still in middle school, takes over the bass
years.p: Tom Front quits after the Harder They Fall demo. Leon is the younger brother of guitarist Aaron Melnick, and Chris Smith arrives from False Hope on second guitar.

years.h: Critics say Those Who Fear Tomorrow will ruin hardcore
years.p: Integrity's debut on Overkill Records bolts metal solos and chugging riffs onto hardcore. It turned into a blueprint for metalcore, and Loudwire put it on its 2020 list of the top 25 metalcore albums.
years.xp: Wikipedia calls it one of the earliest cornerstones of metalcore. The warnings went unheeded: bands that came after took on its darker, metal-leaning sound.

eras.title: Three albums in three years
eras.text: With the Melnick brothers, Chris Smith and Mark Konopka, Integrity signed to Victory Records and kept getting bigger and stranger. Hellion's doomsday cults, occult texts and Charles Manson moved to the center.

years.h: A stopgap EP, Den of Iniquity, before the Victory albums
years.p: It sits between the Overkill debut and the Victory records. The Hooked, Lung, Stolen Breath Cunt EP follows in 1994.

years.h: Outface's Mark Konopka takes the drum stool
years.p: Tony Pines had left after the debut and David Nicholi Araca filled in. Konopka, from the Cleveland band [[Outface|2fabef87-f53f-4792-b05b-6d54a8517d4c]], completes the line-up fans call classic Integrity.

yt: Dwid Hellion on why Systems Overload got remixed (Aggressive Tendencies)
years.h: Systems Overload opens the Victory years
years.p: The classic line-up's first album for Victory. Decibel inducted it into its Hall of Fame in November 2013, calling it "the landmark work in a grand and heretical oeuvre."
years.xp:
Chris Smith helped write the material, Decibel says, and [[Frank Novinec|b7befdca-a6f9-4440-8d24-95611017537a]] was around for the recording and joined soon after.

The album was remixed for its A389 Recordings reissue. Aaron Melnick told Vice he spent days on the mix so the rhythm guitars could be heard better than on the 1995 pressing, and Hellion explains the remix on camera in the video below.

years.h: Frank Novinec, now of Hatebreed, joins on guitar
years.p: Novinec, who also played in Ringworm and [[Terror|697eba1a-bf52-46b1-a19f-4d7190b63e5c]], comes in after the Systems Overload sessions. In 2006 he joins [[Hatebreed|40b7efb7-1268-4a80-b354-600afdcbe9e2]], and he's still there two decades on.

years.h: Kids cut Dwid Hellion's mic cord, and the whole room chases them
years.p: Aaron Melnick told Vice about a Cleveland show where antagonistic kids cut the cable and waited outside for the band. The entire room emptied after them and chased them down the street.

years.h: Charles Manson, from prison, backs Humanity Is the Devil
years.p: Dwid Hellion on Manson, whom he also called a political prisoner and a religious martyr. The album draws on the Process Church of the Final Judgement, and Manson's head went into the Integrity logo.
years.xp:
Manson, writing to Hellion from prison, endorsed the record. Hellion kept up a personal relationship with him and released recordings Manson made inside.

Manson turns up again and again as a subject in Integrity songs.

years.h: Seasons in the Size of Days ends the classic run
years.p: The third Victory album in three years pulls in gothic rock, industrial and noise. The Melnick brothers, Chris Smith and Mark Konopka won't record together again until 2013.

eras.title: Integ2000, then Brussels
eras.text: The classic line-up fell apart, and Hellion rebuilt Integrity with two members of Mushroomhead under a new name. Two Victory albums later he moved to Belgium and took the band with him.

years.h: The Melnicks leave and Mushroomhead's Feltons arrive
years.p: With Aaron and Leon Melnick gone, Dwid Hellion hires brothers Dave and Steve Felton of Cleveland's Mushroomhead plus bassist Craig Martini, and renames the band Integ2000.

years.h: One album as Integ2000
years.p: Integrity 2000 on Victory is the Felton line-up's only record, out the same year as the Final Taste of Every Sin EP.

years.h: Five Victory albums in, Closure is the last
years.p: With the Felton brothers gone, Dwid Hellion drops the Integ2000 name. Invisible Oranges' Neill Jameson later heard a Southern Gothic streak in Closure.

years.h: Dwid Hellion meets a girl on tour and moves to Brussels
years.p: Integrity relocates to Belgium in 2003. Hellion told Thrasher in 2018 that he'd lived in Brussels for about fifteen years.
years.xp: His account: "I was on tour, met a girl, we fell in love and got married."

years.h: To Die For brings Tony Pines back to the drums
years.p: Sold as the comeback, it's Integrity's first album on Deathwish Inc. and reunites Dwid Hellion with founding drummer Tony "Chubby Fresh" Pines.

eras.title: The old five, one night
eras.text: Integrity came back from seven quiet years with a Deathwish album and a Manson single, both made from Belgium. Then the Systems Overload line-up got in a room together for the first time in two decades, for one night in Baltimore.

years.cap: Dwid Hellion in the crowd, Baltimore
years.h: After seven quiet years, The Blackest Curse
years.p: Integrity's second album for Deathwish Inc., the label run by [[Converge|fa31e7d4-a03a-4110-98fc-f8826e95ec25]]'s [[Jacob Bannon|d5c2a3e1-a52a-4af6-8e3f-aa2c4dc69af7]], whose band is one of many that name Integrity as an influence.

years.h: A ninth album ships while the old five record together
years.p: Suicide Black Snake, Integrity's ninth, comes out on A389 and Magic Bullet. The same year the Systems Overload line-up records its first new song together in more than twenty years.

years.h: One night in Baltimore, the old five play again
years.p: Dwid Hellion, Aaron and Leon Melnick, Chris Smith and Mark Konopka play A389's tenth anniversary Bash on January 18, their first show together in more than seventeen years. They sell the new 7th Revelation EP weeks early.
years.xp:
A389's Domenic Romeo, guitarist in Pulling Teeth, had asked Aaron Melnick for years. Melnick told Vice "I like the idea of doing one show." A five-week tour was out of the question with a two-year-old daughter at home, and he and Leon were playing in the crossover band Inmates.

7th Revelation: Beyond the Realm of the VVitch came out officially on February 7, 2014. The show was later released as a live album, and Romeo joined Integrity's touring line-up.

eras.title: Relapse, Francis Bacon and a feud settled
eras.text: Integrity landed at Relapse Records with a line-up built around Hellion and drummer Alex Henderson. The records turned conceptual, the archive came out of the vault, and a 1990s grudge ended as a split record.

years.cap: Integrity live, Dwid Hellion up front, 2017
years.h: Howling follows Francis Bacon into a séance
years.p: Integrity's tenth album, on Relapse, puts the painter drunk at a séance in his studio at 7 Reece Mews and walks through occult moments in history. Dwid Hellion called it the band's most metallic record.
years.xp: Domenic Romeo added lap steel and solos Hellion likened to Randy Rhoads. Hellion told Bandcamp Daily he'd known Romeo about 20 years and that Romeo was close enough to tell him off.

years.cap: Dwid Hellion with Domenic Romeo's line-up, 2017
q: I am a black sheep in hardcore.
years.h: Dwid Hellion's office is stacked with Air Jordan 1s
years.p: Hellion wears only Nike Air Jordan 1s. His father once bought ten pairs at $10 each, which lasted him into his mid-twenties, and he now keeps boxes stacked to the ceiling.

years.h: Integrity and Krieg split an EP on Relapse
years.p: Integrity shares the split with the American black metal band Krieg, another step away from hardcore.

years.h: Relapse opens the vault
years.p: All Death Is Mine: Total Domination collects archival Integrity material. Dwid Hellion keeps rotating guitarists: Asa Dunn joins in 2024 and Harley McCoy in 2025.

years.h: Hellion and Skarhead's Ezec bury a '90s feud on a split 12"
years.p: Dwid Hellion and Skarhead's Danny "Ezec" Singer had no love for each other in the 1990s. They started messaging online, and the result is a split on Static Era Records, with Integrity's Devil Down.
years.xp:
No Echo skips the specifics of the old feud. Hellion's account of the end of it: "Danny and I were messaging each other and the idea to put together a split record materialized from those conversations." Ezec then asked Static Era's owner Jay Reason to release it.

The two also bonded over jokes about Chubby Fresh of One Life Crew, the nickname of Integrity's own founding drummer Tony Pines. Hellion sings on Skarhead's Till' Death We Part too.
